series: 50 MOST ASKED API INTERVIEW QUESTIONS — PART 2

blocks.text: Q26. How does HTTP caching work with Cache-Control, ETag and Last-Modified?
The server sets `Cache-Control` to say how long a response stays ==fresh==. Once stale, the client revalidates with an `ETag` or `Last-Modified` validator.

blocks.title: Key points
items: `max-age=300` reuses the copy for 5 minutes, no request
`ETag` is a version fingerprint, `Last-Modified` a timestamp
`Last-Modified` is only accurate to the **second**
`public` allows shared caches, `private` the browser only

blocks.text: Q27. What is the difference between no-cache and no-store?
`no-cache` may store the response but must ==revalidate== before every reuse. `no-store` forbids keeping any copy at all.

blocks.title: Key points
items: `no-cache` still saves bandwidth through 304 replies
`no-store` is for bank pages, tokens and personal data
**Mistake**: reading `no-cache` as "never cache"

blocks.text: Q28. What is the difference between client-side, CDN and server-side (Redis) caching?
Each layer sits closer to a different party: the user's device, the edge near the user, or your app's data tier. A request hits the nearest layer first.

blocks.title: Key points
items: Browsers can't be purged, so version files: `app.3f9a.js`
A CDN only caches responses marked `public`
Redis is shared by every app server instance

blocks.text: Q29. How do conditional requests and 304 Not Modified save bandwidth?
The client sends its validator in `If-None-Match`. If nothing changed, the server answers ==304== with headers only and no body.

blocks.title: Key points
items: It saves the body bytes, **not** the round trip
`If-Modified-Since` is the timestamp twin of `If-None-Match`
`If-Match` on writes returns `412` on a stale update

blocks.text: ☆ Q31. What is an API gateway?
A ==gateway== is the single front door that sits before your services and handles cross-cutting work, so each service does not.

items: **Routing** `/orders` and `/users` to services
Auth, rate limits, TLS termination
Request/response transforms, caching
Logging, metrics, tracing in one place

blocks.text: ☆ Q32. Gateway vs load balancer?
A load balancer spreads traffic across __identical__ instances; a gateway understands the API and picks a __different__ service per route.

blocks.title: In practice
blocks.text: They stack: gateway in front, a load balancer behind each service.
☆ Q33. Webhooks vs polling?

items: Webhook = server `POST`s to your URL on an event
Use polling when you can't expose a public URL
Best combo: webhook, plus a slow poll as backup

blocks.text: ☆ Q34. Idempotency-Key on POST?
The client sends a unique ==Idempotency-Key== per intent; the server stores the first result and replays it on any retry.

items: Store key, request hash, response
Insert key atomically (unique index)
Expire keys after ~24 hours

blocks.text: Delivery is ==at-least-once==: the sender retries until it sees a 2xx, so the same event can arrive twice.
☆ Q35. Secure, reliable webhooks?

items: Sign body with **HMAC-SHA256** and a shared secret
Check timestamp to block replay attacks
Retry non-2xx with exponential backoff
Dedupe on event `id`; reply 2xx fast

blocks.note: Verify the raw body, not parsed JSON

blocks.text: ☆ Retry schedule
☆ Dedupe by event id

items: Verify the signature first, then dedupe
Insert the event id with a unique index
Process in a queue, ack the sender fast
Keep ids for as long as retries last

blocks.title: Key points
items: Reply 2xx within seconds; do heavy work async
Out-of-order events: compare timestamps or versions
Rotate secrets with two valid signatures at once
Allow only HTTPS endpoints; block private IPs (SSRF)

blocks.text: ☆ What the sender reads
☆ Testing webhooks

items: Replay saved events from the provider dashboard
Tunnel localhost with ngrok for local tests
Send duplicates and out-of-order events on purpose
Trusting a payload without checking the signature
Comparing signatures with plain `==`
Doing slow work before replying 2xx

blocks.title: Interview tip
blocks.text: Say "sign, retry, dedupe": three words that cover secure, reliable webhooks.

blocks.title: Same idea twice
blocks.text: Retries are inevitable, so make every handler safe to run twice.
Q36. What are the API versioning strategies and their trade-offs?
==Versioning== lets old clients keep working while the API changes. Pick one of three places for the version: the **URL path**, a **header**, or a **query** parameter.

blocks.title: Key points
items: URL path is the most common and easiest to debug
Header keeps URLs clean but is hidden from browsers
Query param is easy to add but caches badly
Version only on breaking changes, not every release

blocks.text: Q37. How do you make backward-compatible changes and deprecate a version?
Only **add** things: new optional fields and endpoints, never remove or rename. To retire a version, announce it, send `Deprecation` and `Sunset` headers, then switch it off on the date.

blocks.q: Key points: safe changes and sunset
a_bullets: Safe: add optional fields, new endpoints, new enum values
Breaking: remove, rename, retype, or make a field required
Clients must ignore unknown fields (tolerant reader)
Watch v1 traffic per client, then email before the sunset

blocks.text: Q38. How do you handle large file uploads (multipart, chunked, presigned URLs)?
Small files go as `multipart/form-data` through the API. Big files are split into **chunks** or sent **straight to object storage** with a presigned URL, so the API never carries the bytes.

blocks.title: Key points
items: Presigned URL: API signs, client PUTs directly to S3
Chunked: upload parts, retry only the failed part
Cap size, check type, and scan before trusting a file
Return 202 or a callback once processing finishes

blocks.text: Q39. What is the difference between unit, integration and contract tests?

**Unit** tests check one function with its dependencies faked. **Integration** tests run the API against a real database. **Contract** tests check that consumer and provider agree on the request and response shape.

blocks.title: Key points
items: Many unit tests, fewer integration tests (test pyramid)
Contract tests catch breaking changes without a full stack
Pact: the consumer writes the contract, the provider verifies it

blocks.q: Q40. How do you test an API with mocks, Postman or automated CI checks?
a_bullets: Short answer: mock slow or external services, script requests in Postman, and run all of it on every push in CI
Mock third-party APIs so tests are fast and deterministic
Postman collections assert status, schema and latency
CI fails the build, so a broken API never merges

blocks.text: ☆ What every API test checks

items: Status code matches the contract (201, 404, 422)
Response body matches the schema, no extra fields
Auth failures return 401 or 403, never 200
Error cases: bad input, missing fields, duplicates

blocks.text: ☆ Contract tests in four steps

items: Consumer test records the calls it needs
Pact file is published to a broker
Provider replays the file against real code
A mismatch blocks the deploy in CI

blocks.text: ☆ Common test mistakes

items: Testing only the happy path, never a 4xx
Hitting a live third-party API in CI
Sharing one database between test runs
Asserting on field order, not field values

blocks.title: Pin this
blocks.text: Never break v1 silently: add, warn with Sunset, then remove.

blocks.title: Interview tip
blocks.text: Name the pyramid: many unit, some integration, few contract and end-to-end.
Q41. Which metrics matter for an API?
Track the golden signals: ==latency== as percentiles, traffic, **errors** and saturation. Averages hide the slow tail, so alert on p95 and p99.

a_bullets: p50 is typical; p99 is your unluckiest 1% of users
Error rate = 5xx ÷ total requests, per route
Saturation: CPU, memory, DB pool, queue depth
Alert on SLO burn, not on a single spike

blocks.text: Q42. Logs vs metrics vs traces?
Logs record ==events==, metrics count ==numbers== over time, and traces follow **one request** across services.

a_bullets: Logs: detailed and high-volume, best for one failure
Metrics: cheap aggregates for dashboards and alerts
Traces: spans linked by one trace ID
Put the trace ID in every log line

blocks.text: Q43. Timeouts, retries and breakers?
A ==timeout== bounds each call, ==retries== with backoff ride out blips, and a ==circuit breaker== stops calling a dead service.

a_bullets: Set the timeout first, or threads pile up
Backoff 1s, 2s, 4s plus **jitter** avoids retry storms
Retry only idempotent calls (see page 7)
Breaker states: closed, open, half-open

blocks.text: Q44. Why scale out statelessly?
Add identical instances behind a load balancer: ==horizontal scaling==. Servers must be ==stateless== so any instance can serve any request.
Q45. Sync API vs queue-based async?
A ==synchronous== API holds the connection until the work is done. An ==asynchronous== one queues the job, returns at once and reports **later**.
☆ Scaling out checklist

items: No sessions or uploads kept on local disk
Health check endpoint for the load balancer
Config from env vars, same image everywhere
Connection pooling so replicas don't flood the DB
Sticky sessions used to hide stateful code
Retrying non-idempotent calls after a timeout
Scaling the API while the database stays single

a_bullets: Keep sessions in Redis or a signed JWT, not RAM
Local disk and in-memory caches break across nodes
Autoscale on CPU or request rate
The database becomes the next bottleneck
Sync: simple, fast work, caller needs the result now
Async: slow or bursty work; the queue absorbs spikes
Reply 202 Accepted with a status URL
Queues deliver at least once, so make workers idempotent

blocks.text: ☆ Sync vs async at a glance
☆ Horizontal vs vertical scaling
☆ Making a queue worker safe

items: Ack the message only after the work succeeds
Store the job id so a redelivery is skipped
Cap retries, then park it in a dead-letter queue
Alert on queue depth and oldest message age

blocks.title: Pin this
blocks.text: Sync for fast reads, async for slow or bursty work.

blocks.title: Interview tip
blocks.text: Say "stateless, queue, idempotent": the three words behind scalable, reliable APIs.
Q46. How would you design a URL shortener API?
`POST /links` stores a ==unique short code== mapped to the long URL; `GET /{code}` redirects to it. Reads dwarf writes, so cache hot codes.

a_bullets: 7 base62 chars give ~3.5 trillion codes
Code from a counter, or random plus collision check
**302** keeps click analytics; 301 gets cached
Hot codes live in Redis; the DB is the source of truth

blocks.text: Q47. How would you design a payment API that never charges a customer twice?
Require a client-generated ==Idempotency-Key== on every charge and save the first result against it, so retries replay it. See page 7 for the mechanics.

a_bullets: One key per payment intent, stored with a request hash
Same key with a different body is **rejected**
Save the key and the charge in one transaction
On timeout, reconcile via provider webhooks, never re-charge blindly

blocks.title: Interview tip
blocks.text: Say "key, hash, replay": the three steps that stop a double charge.
Q48. How would you design a public rate-limited API with API keys and usage tiers?
Issue one ==API key== per client, map it to a tier, and count requests per key at the gateway. Over the limit returns `429` with `Retry-After` (algorithms on page 5).

items: Store only a **hash** of each key; show it once
Redis counters keyed by key plus time window
Allow two active keys during rotation

slides.page_title: Key Rotation, Long Jobs and Notifications

blocks.text: ☆ Key rotation in steps

items: Issue a second key; both stay valid
Client switches its config to the new key
Watch traffic on the old key drop to zero
Revoke the old key and log the date

blocks.title: Pin this
blocks.text: Design questions: state the contract, then idempotency, then failure.

items: Storing raw API keys in the database
Putting keys in URLs, where logs capture them
One shared limit for every tier

blocks.title: Interview tip
blocks.text: Say "key, tier, counter, 429": the four parts of a rate-limited public API.
Q49. How would you design a long-running job API such as video processing or report export?
Never hold the connection open: `POST` returns ==202 Accepted== with a job URL, a worker does the work, and the client polls or gets a webhook.

a_bullets: States: queued, running, succeeded, failed
Status endpoint reports progress and the result link
Webhook callback saves wasteful polling
Expire results and make job creation **idempotent**

blocks.text: Q50. How would you design a notification API that sends to millions of users reliably?
Accept the request, ==enqueue== it, and fan out through queues to per-channel workers. Reliability comes from at-least-once delivery plus dedup.

a_bullets: Return 202; the queue absorbs traffic bursts
Separate queues for push, email and SMS
Retry with backoff, then a **dead-letter** queue
Dedup by notification ID; respect user preferences
